\section[la emoción]{la emoción — emotion; excitement}

\label{lesson:ES-C711-emocion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for tension, then the Spanish for to calm.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la emoción}
\textbf{la emoción} — \textquotedblleft{}emotion; excitement\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¡Qué emoción! Mañana nos vamos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{How exciting! We leave tomorrow.}
\end{quote}

\emph{¡Qué emoción!} — How exciting!

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{emoción} was borrowed from French \emph{émotion} (EtymDB), which goes back to Latin \emph{ēmovēre} \textquotedblleft{}to stir up\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{movēre} \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la emoción}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la emoción}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la emoción}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for tension, then the Spanish for to calm, then say \emph{la emoción} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la emoción mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Emotion; excitement\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[emocionado]{emocionado — excited; moved}

\label{lesson:ES-C711-emocionado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to calm, then the Spanish for emotion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: emocionado}
\textbf{emocionado} — \textquotedblleft{}excited; moved\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Estoy muy emocionado por el viaje.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am very excited about the trip.}
\end{quote}

Used with \emph{estar}. It covers both excited and touched.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{emocionado} is the participle of \emph{emocionar}, built on \emph{emoción}, which was borrowed from French \emph{émotion} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{emocionado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{emocionado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{emocionado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to calm, then the Spanish for emotion, then say \emph{emocionado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does emocionado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Excited; moved\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[emocionante]{emocionante — exciting; moving}

\label{lesson:ES-C711-emocionante}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for emotion, then the Spanish for excited.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: emocionante}
\textbf{emocionante} — \textquotedblleft{}exciting; moving\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fue un partido emocionante.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It was an exciting match.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Emocionante} describes the thing; \emph{emocionado} describes the person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{emocionante} is built on \emph{emocionar} with the ending \emph{-ante}; the verb is made from \emph{emoción}, borrowed from French \emph{émotion} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[emotivo]{emotivo — moving, emotional}

\label{lesson:ES-C711-emotivo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for excited, then the Spanish for exciting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: emotivo}
\textbf{emotivo} — \textquotedblleft{}moving, emotional\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fue una boda muy emotiva.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It was a very moving wedding.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Emotivo} describes the moment; \emph{emocionado} describes the person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{emotivo} is usually explained as a learned word built on Latin \emph{ēmōtus} \textquotedblleft{}stirred up\textquotedblright{}, the participle of \emph{ēmovēre}, from \emph{movēre} \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[conmover]{conmover — to move, to touch (emotionally)}

\label{lesson:ES-C711-conmover}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for exciting, then the Spanish for moving.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: conmover}
\textbf{conmover} — \textquotedblleft{}to move, to touch (emotionally)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Su historia me conmovió.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Her story moved me.}
\end{quote}

Stem change: \emph{conmueve}. \emph{Conmovido} — moved, touched.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{conmover} is inherited from Latin \emph{commovēre} \textquotedblleft{}to stir deeply\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{movēre} \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
